paragraphs.text: Wisdom is a [raw pu’er](sheng:identity) from Yunnan, sold loose rather than pressed. It began as leaf from the province’s large-leaf tea trees: picked, withered, then fried in a wok to [kill the green](sheng:making), rolled and dried in the sun. The leaf is never hot-air dried afterwards, so some of its own enzyme activity survives the heat, and that is what lets the tea keep changing for years.

Raw pu’er may be pressed into cakes or [left loose](sheng:processing), and this tea was kept as leaf. It was never given the quick fermentation of shou, so it [changes slowly in storage](sheng:aging), and the conditions it is kept in become part of its history.

brewing.text: Young raw pu’er takes water a little off the boil, about 85 to 95°C, because hotter water draws out more of its bitterness; an aged one takes 95°C to boiling. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and a quick rinse of a few seconds, then a first steep of ten to fifteen seconds, adding a few seconds each round. A good raw tea gives eight to ten cups or more.

notice.text: In young raw pu’er, a bitter, drying bite that turns into a returning sweetness, a feel in the throat that makes the mouth water, and fresh, floral or fruity notes such as apricot or plum. Tea kept in humid storage can carry a damp, earthy storage taste.
